Objective Acute single strenuous exercise increases circulating cell free DNA (cf DNA). We tested whether three repeated bouts of exhaustive exercise induced the cf DNA response without development of tolerance in healthy men. Methods Eleven average-trained men (age 34.0±5.2 years, body mass index 26.2±3.1 kg/m2, maximal oxygen consumption—VO 2 max 49.6±4.5 ml/kg*min) performed three treadmill exercise tests to exhaustion at speed corresponding to 70% VO 2 max separated by 72 hours of resting. Blood was collected before and after each bout of exercise for determination of cell free nuclear and mitochondrial DNA (cf n-DNA, cf mt-DNA) by real-time PCR, selected markers of muscle damage, and blood cell count. Results Each bout induced the increase (p<0.05) in plasma cf n-DNA: from 3.4±1.4 to 38.5±27.5, from 4.1±3.3 to 48.5±26.2, and 3.1±1.6 to 53.8±39.9 ng/mL after the first, second, and third exercise, respectively. In a congruent way, cf mt-DNA rose significantly after the second (from 229±216 to 450±228*103 GE/mL) and third bout of exercise (from 173±120 to 462±314*103 GE/mL). Pre-exercise cf mt-DNA decreased (p<0.05) by 2-times (from 355±219 before the first bout to 173±120*103 GE/mL before the third bout) over the study period and were accompanied by significant increase in white blood cells, platelets, creatine kinase, creatinine and lactate after each bout. However, the exercise induced percentage increment of cf n-DNA was always many times higher than corresponding increments of the afore-mentioned markers at any occasion. Conclusions Repeated bouts of exhaustive exercise induced remarkable increase in circulating cf n-DNA without signs of tolerance development. Baseline cf mt-DNA decreased in response to series of strenuous exercise. Since percentage increments of cf n-DNA in response to exercise were many times higher than those observed for other markers, measurement of circulating cf n-DNA could be a sensitive tool for monitoring acute exercise effects in human body. http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/501100005888 Uniwersytet Medyczny w Lodzi 503/1-079-01/503-11-001 Nowak Dariusz This study was supported by a research grant from Medical University of Lodz, no. 503/1-079-01/503-11-001. Introduction Repeated bouts of exercise are an effective impulse for physiological adaptation. Skeletal muscle reveals notable plasticity in functional adaptation and remodeling in response to acute or chronic physical activity. Training-induced adaptations are reflected by changes in the contractile proteins, mitochondrial function, metabolic regulation, intracellular signaling, and transcriptional response [ 1 ]. Prolonged endurance training elicits a variety of metabolic and morphological changes, including mitochondrial biogenesis, muscle fiber type transformation, increased capilarization, improved regulation of K+, H+ and lactate ions, and more efficient substrate metabolism [ 2 , 3 ]. However, extensive training can also be accompanied by some adverse effects associated with the inflammatory response. Lactic acid accumulation and damage to muscle fibers may induce the rise in plasma activities of certain enzymes including creatine kinase (CK), asparate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), as well as the elevation of circulating cell free DNA [ 4 , 5 ]. Cell free DNA (cf DNA) can be divided in two polls according to its origin: cell free nuclear DNA (cf n-DNA) and cell free mitochondrial DNA (cf mt-DNA), deriving from nucleus or cytoplasmic mitochondria’s, respectively. Increased levels of circulating cf n-DNA were observed under variety of pathological conditions including cancer, autoimmune diseases, stroke, traumatic brain, and other organs injury [ 6 – 10 ]. In contrast to the afore-mentioned pathological conditions, exercise-induced increase in cf n-DNA is transient [ 11 – 13 ], probably due to the parallel elevation of serum DNAse 1 activity leading to its normalization within 0.5 to 2 hours of recovery [ 13 ]. Moreover, exercise-induced increase in cf n-DNA is not specific to sport disciplines, however, seems to be strictly related to the load of physical exertion [ 7 – 14 ]. On the other hand, studies on the association between exercise and circulating levels of cf mt-DNA gave controversial results. Exhaustive exercises related to 10 km cross-country run and treadmill running workout did not alter plasma cf mt-DNA levels [ 15 , 16 ], while in other trials involving treadmill runners and professional male volleyball players, exercise surprisingly caused the decline in cf mt-DNA [ 17 ]. Although the cellular source of exercise-induced cf DNA is still an unresolved question (apoptotic or necrotic cells, skeletal muscles, blood mononuclear cells, cells of the hematopoietic lineage) [ 18 , 19 ], this phenomenon is supposed to be the predictor of muscle damage, immunological alterations, inflammatory response, and even the overtraining syndrome in elite athletes [ 6 – 14 ]. However, the intensity of cf DNA response to the repeated bouts of strenuous exercise has not been studied so far. One may suppose that due to some adaptive processes these cf DNA responses would decline in the order of appearance. Therefore, in this study we wanted to determine the effect of three repeated exhaustive treadmill runs (separated each by 3 days of recovery) on cf n-DNA and cf mt-DNA plasma levels in healthy physically active young men. Furthermore, the intensity of cf DNA response was compared with the exercise-induced rise in white blood cells (WBC), circulating levels of lactic acid, creatinine and activities of AST, ALT and CK.

core_effect_and_quantification.biomarker_name: circulating cell free nuclear DNA (cf n-DNA)
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Tremendous increase (more than 10-times), specifically 12.7-fold after first, 17.1-fold after second, and 18.9-fold after third bout. Initial plasma levels were 3.4 0 11.4 ng/mL before the first bout, rising to 38.5 0 127.5, 48.5 0 126.2, and 53.8 0 139.9 ng/mL after the first, second, and third bouts respectively (p<0.05). This increment was many times higher than other markers.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Repeated bouts of exhaustive treadmill exercise
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Lactic acid accumulation and muscle fiber damage contribute to increased plasma enzyme activities (CK, AST, ALT) and circulating cell free DNA (cf DNA). The rapid increase in cf n-DNA suggests its release from living cells, possibly including neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and DNA derived from hematopoietic cell lineages like neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes. Exercise-induced cf DNA is considered a predictor of muscle damage, immunological alterations, inflammatory response, and overtraining syndrome. Post-exercise cf mt-DNA increase may stem from mitochondrial DNA release by white blood cells (e.g., neutrophils, activated platelets) and leakage of biomolecules from mitochondria. Reduced renal and visceral blood flow during strenuous exercise might also lower cf DNA clearance. The observed pre-exercise decline in cf mt-DNA could be due to increased mt-DNA fragment clearance, inhibition of baseline mt-DNA release, or greater sensitivity to DNAse degradation, hypothesizing a biphasic effect (stimulation then inhibition during rest).

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Repeated bouts of exhaustive exercise induced a remarkable and consistent increase in circulating cf n-DNA without signs of tolerance development. Conversely, baseline cf mt-DNA decreased by two-times over the study period in response to the series of strenuous exercise. Baseline creatine kinase (CK) levels showed a significant increasing trend across the three repeated exercise bouts, indicating no normalization during 72-hour resting periods. AST and ALT increased significantly only after the third bout. Lactate and creatinine raised significantly after each bout, with stable baseline levels. Urea, glucose, and C-reactive protein showed significant increases only after the first bout. Run distance to exhaustion was shorter at the first bout compared to the subsequent two bouts (p<0.05). More intense exercise (potentially equivalent to a half-marathon) appeared to stimulate increased cf mt-DNA release, unlike prolonged moderate exercise which led to a decrease.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The exercise-induced percentage increment of cf n-DNA was always many times higher (several dozen-times) than corresponding increments of white blood cells, platelets, creatine kinase, creatinine, AST, and ALT, making it a highly sensitive indicator for acute exercise-induced changes. Lactic acid's percentage increase was approximately half to one-fourth of that seen for cf n-DNA. Plasma or serum analyses were corrected for hematocrit shifts to specifically account for dehydration effects, enhancing specificity.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Eleven apparently healthy, average-trained men (age 25-45 years, mean 34.0 0 15.2 years; mean body mass index 26.2 0 13.1 kg/m 0 12; maximal oxygen consumption—VO2max 49.6 0 14.5 ml/kg*min).
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Circulating cf n-DNA could serve as a highly sensitive tool for monitoring acute exercise effects in the human body, acting as a predictor of muscle damage, immunological alterations, inflammatory response, and overtraining syndrome in athletes. Repeated exhaustive treadmill exercise induces a significant physiological stress response characterized by a notable rise in cf n-DNA and a moderate increase in cf mt-DNA, alongside markers of skeletal muscle damage and metabolic reactions. The novel observation of gradually decreasing pre-exercise cf mt-DNA levels over the study period provides further insight into physiological adaptation.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic utility, physiological response characterization, and monitoring tool for stress/damage.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Measurement of circulating cf n-DNA is described as a highly sensitive and reliable tool, with a rapid response (within 9 minutes) and percentage increments many times higher than other measured markers. The elevated cf n-DNA response is transient, returning to baseline within 72 hours of resting, and pre-exercise cf n-DNA levels were stable. cf mt-DNA also showed a moderate, transient increase, though its pre-exercise levels gradually decreased over the study period. Reliability of plasma/serum analysis was enhanced by correcting for hematocrit shifts caused by exercise-induced water loss. The observed effects were consistent across all subjects, and the study size (n=11) was sufficient to demonstrate significant changes, though it limited correlation calculations. The consistency with previous studies regarding the magnitude of cf n-DNA increase further supports reliability.
recommended_alternatives: Further clinical studies are needed to precisely determine the contribution of neutrophils and monocytes to the increase in circulatory cf n-DNA induced by repeated exercises.
